# Part 2 — Matrix Setup and Standardization

```{python}
pred_cols = ["size_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]

predictors = df[pred_cols].to_numpy()
y = df["price_thousands"].to_numpy()

means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (predictors - means) / sds
```

Check that the standardized columns have mean about 0 and standard deviation 1:

```{python}
print("Column means of Z:", np.round(Z.mean(axis=0), 10))
print("Column SDs of Z:  ", np.round(Z.std(axis=0), 10))
```

```{python}
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])

shape_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": [
        "predictors", "Z", "X", "y",
        "matrix rank of X",
        "number of predictors (excluding intercept)",
    ],
    "Value": [
        str(predictors.shape), str(Z.shape), str(X.shape), str(y.shape),
        str(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)),
        str(Z.shape[1]),
    ],
})
shape_table
```

**Written response.**
`X` and `y` must have compatible shapes because the model `y ≈ Xβ`
requires the number of rows in `X` to equal the number of observations in
`y`. Otherwise `X @ beta` and the residuals `y - X @ beta` cannot be
computed. The intercept column of ones lets the model estimate a baseline
level (the predicted price when all standardized predictors are at their
means) instead of forcing the fitted surface through the origin.
Standardizing put all three predictors on a common scale with mean 0 and
standard deviation 1, so their coefficients can be compared directly.
Broadcasting makes this possible without a loop because NumPy stretches
the length-3 vectors `means` and `sds` across every row of the `(n, 3)`
matrix, so `(predictors - means) / sds` is applied to each column at once.
